titleText.es: Estoy enseñándole a decir esto a todo familiar de 8 años que tengo, y a todos los de 14 años a decir lo mismo de Toy Story. Además, Pokemom llegó a EEUU hace más de una década y los niños que nacieron después de que saliera Aladdin cumplirán 18 el año que viene.
titleText.en: I'm teaching every 8-year-old relative to say this, and every 14-year-old to do the same thing with Toy Story.  Also, Pokemon hit the US over a decade ago and kids born after Aladdin came out will turn 18 next year.
titleText.noteEn: The English title text is copied exactly from official xkcd, including its two-space sentence break. The Spanish archive has the genuine spelling Pokemom and otherwise adapts the same generation-gap examples. In the raster, 11S is the Spanish alphanumeric shorthand for the September 11 attacks and ROB is an unchanged proper name, so both are explicitly inventoried but not made vocabulary cards.

regions.labelEs: PERO ¡NUNCA ENCONTRARON LA CABEZA DEL FANTASMA!
UNA HISTORIA MUY CHORRA, TÍO ROB.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the unchanged personal name of the uncle, not Spanish vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: ¿Y TÚ TIENES UNA QUE DÉ MÁS MIEDO?

applications.explanationEn: Una leaves the feminine thing unidentified, and que introduces dé in the special form used for the sought scarier example.
Dé supplies the matching form of dar for the unspecified story, while miedo names the fear it would cause.
Intenta is the affirmative informal singular command of intentar.
Lo attaches to the affirmative command intenta, and the written accent preserves the original stress.

regions.labelEs: EL 11S SUCEDIÓ ANTES DE QUE YO NACIERA, Y SIN EMBARGO TENGO EDAD SUFICIENTE PARA MANTENER ESTA CONVERSACIÓN CONTIGO.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the alphanumeric Spanish shorthand for the September 11 attacks, not a lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Antes de que places the speaker's birth after the earlier event, and naciera uses the special past-looking subjunctive form for that later event.
Sin embargo marks the age statement as a contrast with having been born after the earlier event.
Tengo matches the speaker, edad suficiente para expresses being old enough, and mantener stays in its unchanged dictionary form for the resulting action.
Mantener combines with conversación to describe carrying on the exchange; esta identifies which conversation without changing the expression's core words.

cards.noteEn: Encontraron is the completed-past form of encontrar for they or formal plural you. The stem stays encontr- and the -aron ending marks an -ar verb's completed plural action.

example.en: They found the keys yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: Fantasma ends in -a but is normally masculine when it names a ghost: el fantasma.

example.en: The castle has a ghost.

cards.noteEn: Chorra is an informal Spain description for something foolish, trivial, or unimpressive. It is the feminine singular form, used with a feminine naming word such as historia.

example.en: It was a really lame excuse.

cards.noteEn: Tío literally means an uncle. Before a relative's name in direct address, it functions like the English family title “Uncle.” This is distinct from the informal Spain use meaning “guy.”

example.en: Thanks, Uncle Carlos.

cards.noteEn: Una can stand on its own for one feminine person or thing when the noun is already understood. It is not introducing a new noun in this use.

example.en: I want one that is comfortable.

cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive after que when describing that unknown person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Spanish treats a known person differently from one you are still trying to find. Conozco a alguien que habla inglés means “I know someone who speaks English.” Busco a alguien que hable inglés uses hable because no particular person has been identified.
cards.questionEn: Which verb form do you use when you are looking for a person or thing that has not been identified—and may not exist?

example.es: Busco a alguien que hable inglés.
example.en: I am looking for someone who speaks English.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: gives; causes (special form for a sought scary thing)
cards.noteEn: Dé is a form of dar. The accent distinguishes it from the preposition de. Here the speaker asks about an unspecified story that might cause more fear, so dar appears in this special subjunctive form.

example.es: Busco una película que dé miedo.
example.en: I am looking for a movie that is scary.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is scary or frightens someone?
cards.answerEn: Name the scary thing, use the matching form of dar, and add miedo. Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les when you need to name who feels afraid.
cards.noteEn: Spanish presents the source of fear as “giving fear.” Dar changes for that source; miedo stays unchanged. The small person marker identifies who feels the fear and can be omitted for a general statement.

example.en: Thunder scares me.

cards.noteEn: Intenta is the affirmative command for one familiar person, and lo stands for the thing to try. Lo attaches to the command, and the written accent keeps the original stress: inténtalo.

example.en: Try it again.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

example.en: Sit down here!

cards.noteEn: Sucedió is the completed-past form of suceder for one event or thing.

example.en: The change happened in April.

cards.promptEs: 11S · antes de nacer · edad suficiente para conversar
cards.answerEn: the frightening realization that someone born after the September 11 attacks is already old enough to hold a conversation
cards.noteEn: The September 11 attacks occurred in 2001, while this comic appeared in 2009. The child's line compresses that growing time gap into an ordinary conversation and makes the older relative feel the passage of time more sharply than the ghost story did. The title text extends the same joke to younger relatives and older popular culture.
Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

example.en: Call me before you leave.

cards.questionEn: How do you connect one event to a later event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de que, then put the pending event's verb in the subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used after this connector because the later event has not happened yet. For regular -ar verbs, this form uses an e ending: lanzar becomes lance. If one person performs both actions, Spanish often uses antes de plus the second verb's unchanged dictionary form instead: como antes de salir means “I eat before leaving.”

example.en: Leave before it rains.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: De is a required middle piece when antes introduces a full event with que. Translate antes de que as one connector.

example.en: Let's return before it gets dark.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes antes de que (“before”)
cards.noteEn: Que completes the connector before a full event. The following verb uses a special pending-event form called the subjunctive.

example.en: Eat before they arrive.

cards.answerEn: was born (special form after antes de que)
cards.noteEn: Naciera is a past-looking subjunctive form of nacer. Antes de que uses this form because the birth is viewed as the later event relative to what happened before it.

example.es: La casa existía antes de que yo naciera.
example.en: The house existed before I was born.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cards.noteEn: Sin normally means “without,” but sin embargo is one fixed connector. In that expression, translate the pair together rather than translating sin separately.

example.en: I wanted to go out; however, it was raining.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a contrast with “however” or “nevertheless”?
cards.answerEn: Use sin embargo before or after the contrasting idea.
cards.noteEn: Sin embargo functions as one fixed connector. Its meaning is not obtained by translating sin as “without” and embargo separately. A comma often separates it from the rest of the statement.

example.es: Está cansada; sin embargo, continúa trabajando.
example.en: She is tired; however, she keeps working.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cards.noteEn: In sin embargo, embargo does not contribute a separate English word. The two Spanish words work together as the connector “however” or “nevertheless.”

example.es: Es difícil; sin embargo, es posible.
example.en: It is difficult; however, it is possible.

cards.answerEn: I am (stating age); literally, I have
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses tener, “to have,” when stating age. Tengo is the form for the speaker: tengo edad suficiente means “I am old enough.”

example.en: I am twenty years old.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is old enough to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of tener, then edad suficiente para and the action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Tener changes for the person: tengo, tienes, tiene, and so on. Edad suficiente para stays together, and the following -ar, -er, or -ir verb does not change.

example.es: Ya tiene edad suficiente para viajar solo.
example.en: He is old enough to travel alone now.

cards.noteEn: Suficiente describes an adequate amount or degree. After neutral lo, lo suficiente means “enough” or “what is sufficient.”

example.en: That is enough.

cards.answerEn: to; enough for the following action
cards.noteEn: After suficiente, para introduces the action that the amount, ability, or age is enough to perform. The following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: There is enough light to read.

cards.answerEn: to carry on; to have (a conversation)
cards.noteEn: Mantener often means “to keep” or “to maintain.” With conversación, it describes having or carrying on the exchange.

example.es: Es fácil mantener una conversación con ella.
example.en: It is easy to carry on a conversation with her.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that people have or carry on a conversation?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of mantener with conversación, or conversaciones for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Mantener literally often means to keep or maintain, but with conversación it describes having or carrying on the exchange. Mantener changes with the person and time; for example, yo mantengo and estamos manteniendo.

example.en: We have a calm conversation.

cards.noteEn: Spanish combines con and ti into the special single word contigo.

example.en: I want to talk with you.
